catalog_quote: For words uttered in isolation and short phrases, the penultimate stress pattern is pervasive; it holds for bi-, tri- and the occasional quadrisyllabic lexical item, as shown in (69), (70) and (71), respectively. [...] Penultimate stress also applies to disyllabic grammatical items. [...] Note that lexical items in which more than one syllable precedes the stress-bearing one (as in the quadrisyllables in (71) above) have a secondary stress on the first syllable (thus [ˌisaˈrami] 'elder brother', [ˌusuˈpadu] 'candle' and [ˌɾaɾaˈnini] 'decoration'). This yields a trochaic rhythm. [...] A notable set of exceptions to this trochaic pattern is presented by words or short phrases ending in heavy syllables. (73) gives some examples with diphthongs, while those in (74) have long vowels. (73) [ˌkamuˈnɛi] kamunei 'noon' / [ˌdadaˈwai] dada-uai 'grandfather (HON)' (74) [ˌlɛtɛˈrɔː] leteroo 'coarse bag' / [ˌsɔtɛˈmɛː] sotemee 'self, alone' The defining feature of heavy syllables is that they consist of two morae, as shown in (75) for kamunei 'tomorrow' and leteroo 'coarse bag', respectively. [p. 91] Clearly, Makalero makes use of the moraic trochee as defined by Ewen and van der Hulst (2001: 227) [...] This system thus bases the notion of foot on moraic rather than syllabic structure, such that a foot must consist of two morae rather than two syllables. The word stress thus lies on the last foot rather than on the penultimate syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (700 PDF pages; the PDF's metadata gives the Author "Juliette Huber"; cover reads "A grammar of Makalero / A Papuan language of East Timor"; the LOT URLhttps://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/279_fulltext.pdfanswers HTTP 200 with the same 3,115,155-byte file, so the source is open). The text is garbage (no ToUnicode map), so I rendered pp. 114-115 to PNG and read the page scan directly: they carry printed page numbers 90 and 91, section 2.6.1. Every clause of the reported quote is on those pages word for word: p. 90 "For words uttered in isolation and short phrases, the penultimate stress pattern is pervasive; it holds for bi-, tri- and the occasional quadrisyllabic lexical item, as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress falls on the rightmost moraic trochee, built right to left: on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (fala, lolitu, isarami, and disyllabic grammatical items), but on the final syllable when it is heavy (diphthong or long vowel: kamunei, leteroo). Effectively stress on the penultimate mora. Feet are left-headed; a leftover initial light syllable is stranded.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of quadrisyllables and of words with a heavy final ([,isa'rami], [,usu'padu], [,kamu'nei]); an initial heavy syllable forms its own foot and carries its own (secondary or near-equal) stress ([,pu:'lata] 'head', [,mi:'tini]).
new_statements.exceptions: Words/short phrases ending in heavy syllables (diphthong or long vowel) take final main stress (kamunei [,kamu'nei], leteroo [,lete'ro:], p. 90). Words with an initial heavy syllable show an extra stress on it (puulata [,pu:'lata], mit=ini [,mi:'tini], loans viitima, saapatu, p. 92-93), interpreted as compounds/multi-morphemic. Loanwords may keep donor-language stress via vowel length (viitima 'victim', p. 93).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain: isolated words and short phrases (§2.6.1); beyond the morpheme the domain of stress assignment is the phonological word, clitics like =ini and =ee can take or shift stress (§2.6.2, pp. 93-94), and stress in longer utterances is described as variable and not fully analysed. Stress is realised mainly through intensity, not length or pitch (p. 87-89). Echo vowels count as morae and shift stress (asan ['ʔasan] vs [a'sa:na], p. 92). 'I am not aware of minimal pairs with stress as the only distinctive feature.' (p. 93)
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's language-level maka1316 'Makasae-Makalero' has two dialects: Makasai [maka1317] and Maklere (= Makalero) [makl1245]. The quoted statement (Huber 2011) describes Makalero of Iliomar subdistrict, i.e. makl1245. Makasae proper (maka1317) has the same pattern in two first-hand open sources saved alongside: Fogaça 2015, pp. 81-82: 'Em Makasae, o acento é previsível na penúltima sílaba [..] quando a última sílaba é considerada pesada, o acento recai sobre ela, sendo assim classificado como sensível à quantidade (SQ)' ('In Makasae stress is predictable on the penultimate syllable.. when the final syllable is heavy, stress falls on it, so it is classified as quantity-sensitive'); and Brotherson 2003, p. 23: 'Primary stress in native Makasai words is usually placed on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stress on the preantepenultimate syllable.' So the weight-sensitive penultimate-mora reading holds for both dialects of maka1316.

new_statements.quote: "Makasae is delivered with syllable-timed rhythm. It does not have an obvious expiratory accent, but certain syllables in an utterance stand out on account of their higher pitch. It appears that in Makasae, as in its close relative Fataluku, tone is lexical. A word may have a prominent syllable, usually the second or first, marked by higher pitch than the surrounding syllables [...]" (p. 24) "Makasae stress is naturally labile, hence in contrast with Tetum, most Makasae polysyllabic words are stressed equally (15). However, when a speaker emphasises a word, the penultimate syllable is usually lengthened (16)." (p. 31)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's existing statement (Huber 2011, Makalero of Iliomar) has pervasive penultimate stress in isolation, secondary stress on the first syllable of longer words, and final heavy (bimoraic) syllables attracting stress (moraic trochee, catalog reading weight-sensitive). Correia instead describes NO obvious expiratory stress ('most Makasae polysyllabic words are stressed equally'), with pitch prominence 'usually [on] the second or first' syllable and a tentative claim that 'tone is lexical' -- a different prosodic type, not merely a different placement. Two caveats on the contradiction: (a) Correia describes the north-eastern Makasae dialect of Laga and treats Makalero as a separate ne…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For north-eastern (Laga) Makasae, Correia denies an obvious dynamic (expiratory) word stress: rhythm is syllable-timed and most polysyllabic words are 'stressed equally' (examples falunu, hodesara, tufu-berekama, gira-gira transcribed without stress marks); word-level prominence is a higher-pitched syllable, usually the second or the first, which he tentatively takes to be lexical tone / pitch accent as in Fataluku, its realisation depending on sentence intonation. Under emphasis the penultimate vowel is lengthened (oma [ɔːma], dera [deːɾa], omene [omeːne], laihona [laihoːna]). Apparent diphthongs are analysed as sequences of two 'equally stressed' vowels (p. 32). He explicitly declares a full treatment of prosody beyond the scope of the thesis (p. 24-25), so the tonal/pitch accent claim is hedged ('It appears that').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the source denies a regular dynamic stress altogether.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 48 (p. 31), citing Hull, Makasai p. 4: 'certain Makasae speakers whose language is strongly influenced by Tetum tend to stress words as they would in Tetum'. §1.5.2 (p. 8 region): mesolectal speakers 'ignore word stress' of Tetum/Portuguese loanwords. Emphatic pronunciation lengthens the penultimate syllable (p. 31).
new_statements.identity_note: Correia 2011 describes the north-eastern variety of Makasae, dialect of Laga (Baucau district), taken as normative, with occasional notes on Baucau and Ossu forms; he treats Makalero as a distinct neighbouring language (Glottolog 5: Maklere makl1245, a dialect of Makasae-Makalero maka1316, alongside Makasai maka1317). The catalog's existing statement (Huber 2011) is for Makalero specifically; Brotherson 2003 held by the project is Ossu Makasai.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement. Correia 2011 (north-eastern Makasae, Laga dialect; ch. 3, pp. 24-25 and 31-32) says Makasae 'does not have an obvious expiratory accent', that 'most Makasae polysyllabic words are stressed equally', and that prominence is a higher-pitched syllable 'usually the second or first', tentatively lexical tone/pitch accent as in Fataluku -- while the catalog's statement for maka1316 (Huber 2011, Makalero: penultimate stress pervasive in isolation, final heavy syllables stressed, secondary stress on the first syllable; moraic-trochee = weight-sensitive) and the other Makasae sources already checked held by the project (Brotherson 2003 p. 23: penultimate primary stress; Fogaça 2015 §3.7 pp. 81-82: predictable penultimate accent) all describe a regular right-edge (penultimate-based) word stress. Correia's account is explicitly provisional ('It appears that.. tone is lexical'; 'Discussion of Makasae prosody is beyond the scope of this thesis'), gives no minimal pairs for tone, and his 'second or first syllable' pitch peak coincides with the penult in two- and three-syllable words, so the conflict is chiefly about the phonetic nature and regularity of prominence (pitch vs. dynamic stress; 'labile'/equal stress) rather than a rival fixed position. It may also reflect a genuine dialect difference (Laga Makasae vs. Makalero/Ossu Makasai) or Tetum influence, which Correia himself notes (fn. 48).
